Foreign investors have freedom to appoint board members of their choice. Question: description: Patent application issues
Source Legislation: Patents Act No.2 of 2003
Impact: Part 4 of the Act prescribes the application for patents and Part 5 prescribes procedure for granting patent. A person shall filling an application with the Registrar of Patents (Section 12). If the Registrar determines the application does not comply with this Act, the Registrar must inform the applicant and ask to amend the application (Section 16). There is no restrictions related to the application process for patents.

Question: description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
Source Legislation: Patents Act No.2 2003
Impact: Patent enforcement involves both civil and administrative procedures. The patent owner can initiate court proceedings for any alleged infringement (Section 42.1), including an injunction restraining the defendant from any alleged act of infringement (Section 42.2a). Administratively, the Registrar manages the submission, examination, and publication of patent applications, resolves disputes between applicants (Section 21), and has the authority to revoke patents on specific grounds (Section 39). Remedies include injunctions, damages, destruction of infringing products, and declarations of validity and infringement.

Question: description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
Source Legislation: Patents Act No.2 of 2003
Impact:
According to Part 11 of the Act, patent infringement and proceedings are regulated. If a person infringes a patent invention, the owner of a patent may bring proceedings in court for any act alleged to infringe the patent (Section 41). The remedies cover an injunction, damages for the infringement, an account of the profits derived by the defendant from infringement, etc. (Section 42).

There is no restriction or report related to the enforcement of patents.

Question: description: Lack of copyright framework and exceptions
Source Legislation: Copyright and Related Rights Act No. 42 of 2000
Impact:
Under the Copyright and Related Rights Act of 2000, Part 3 Acts Not Constituting Infringement of Copyright in Works, certain acts are not considered an infringement of copyright. The exceptions include fair dealing for purposes of research or private study, legal advise, criticism or review (Sections 10 -18). 

In particular, certain acts that not considered as an infringement are:
1. Private reproduction for personal purposes
2. Temporary reproduction
3. Quotation
4. Reproduction for educational or legal purposes
5. Reproduction by libraries and archives
6. Reproduction, broadcasting and other communication to the public for information purposes
7. Reproduction and adaptation of computer programs
8. Importation for personal purposes
9. Display of works
Timeframe for Indicator: Assented December 2000, commencement February 2011, last amended in November 2021

Question: description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures

Impact: Under Part 6 enforcement of rights and protection requirements, the Supreme Court has jurisdiction in respect of civil and criminal matters arising under the Copyright Act (Sections 34 and 35). A person who intentionally and for profit making purposes infringes a right protected under this Act is guilty of an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding 2,000,000 Vatu or imprisonment for not more than 2 years, or both (Section 35.2). The Court is also authorized to grant injunctions to prohibit the infringement. There have not been recent complaints related to online piracy.
Timeframe for Indicator: Assented December 2000, commencement February 2011, last amended in November 2021

Question: description: Mandatory disclosure of trade secrets, such as source code and algorithms
Source Legislation: Trade Secrets Act of 2000 No.52 of 2000
Impact:
A person who is the owner of a trade secret has the right to that secret remaining undisclosed (Section 2). 

If a trade secret is acquired, used or disclosed by a person without the authority of the owner of the trade secret, the owner has the right to apply to the Supreme Court for a declaration that the trade secret has been acquired, used or disclosed without authority (Section 3). The Supreme Court may grant an injunction and award damages to the owner.

Question: description: Lack of effective trade secrets legal framework
Source Legislation: Trade Secrets Act of 2000 No.52 of 2000
Impact:
The Trade Secrets Act defines a trade secret as any information that is (Section 1):
(a) not generally known among, or readily accessible to, persons who
normally deal with information of that kind; or
(b) about a person’s business or professional affairs and disclosure would, or could reasonably be expected to, unreasonably affect that person adversely in respect of his or her lawful business or professional affairs;  and that has commercial value because of this. 

If a trade secret is acquired, used or disclosed by a person without the authority of the owner of the trade secret, the owner has the right to apply to the Supreme Court for a declaration that the trade secret has been acquired, used or disclosed without authority.  The Court may: grant an injunction preventing anyone from dealing with, or otherwise using, the secret in a commercial way; and if it is satisfied that the owner has suffered damage because of the unauthorised disclosure—award damages to the owner (Section 3).

Question: description: Absence of passive infrastructure sharing
Source Legislation: Telecommunications and Radiocommunications Regulation Act No. 30 of 2009
Impact:
Passive infrastructure sharing is not mandated. 
However, on the Island of Akam, South Malekula, TRBR was entrusted with the task of enhancing mobile coverage on the area of Akam Island and its adjacent mainland area. In collaboration with the Office of the Government Chief Information Officer (OGCIO), TRBR has decided to initiate a pilot project centered around 'Shared Infrastructure' to optimize resources to deliver services to the consumers. This approach entails that the Government will assume ownership of the tower, which will then be leased by the Telcos for using the tower and power.

The Universal Access and infrastructure sharing report 2024 is due to come out soon, and will have further information as to how infrastucture sharing is conducted.

Question: description: Lack of comprehensive legal framework for data protection
Impact:
Comprehensive data protection laws are currently before parliament. Data protection laws can be found in sectoral laws, such as the Electronic Transaction Act (Section 25), the Cybercrime Act, and Telecommunications and Radiocommunications Regulation Act (Section 40). 

Specifically, the Telecommunications Act provides that a service provider must not, without the consent of the end user, divulge any personal end user information to any other person who is not an agent or employee of the service provider, unless required by law or authorised by warrant or by the Regulator (Section 40(1)). A service provider must not, without the consent of the end user, collect any personal end user information not reasonably necessary for the provision of any telecommunications service to the end user, unless required by law or authorised by warrant or by the Regulator (Section 40(2)).

Question: description: Requirements to allow government access to personal data
Source Legislation: Cybercrime Act No.22 of 2021
Impact:
A service provider who receives an order from the Supreme Court relating to a criminal investigation shall disclose the information (Section 15, Disclosure of information of an investigation). The Commissioner of Police must apply to the Court to grant an interception warrant, the renewal of such warrant, or an urgent interception warrant (Sections 27 and 28).

However, the Commissioner of Police is authorized to request a service provider in writing to disclosure subscriber data, or traffic data,  if the disclosure is necessary for law enforcement purposes or a foreign serious offence. A service provider must comply as soon as practical after receiving the request unless shall committed to offence and liable to fine (Sections 21 and 22). Moreover, the Commissioner can request a service provider in writing to access to traffic data in real time for up to 90 days for the enforcement of punishable offence or foreign serious offence (Section 23).

Question: description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
Source Legislation: Electronic Transactions Act No.24 of 2000
Impact:
Intermediaries and e-commerce service providers are not civilly or criminally liable for the content of a message if the intermediary was not the creator of the message, and: (1) the intermediary did not know that dissemination of the message would be grounds for liability; or (2) the intermediary did not know any related facts or circumstances which would have made it reasonable to suspect there was liability; or if the intermediary has complied with Article 27 of the Electronic Transactions Act procedure if the intermediary has become aware of the existence of a civil or criminal penalty, or became aware of facts or circumstances which should have led the intermediary to conclude there was a reasonable likelihood of liability.

Specifically, under this Act, "e-commerce service provider" means a person who uses electronic means in providing goods, services or information, and "intermediary", in relation to an electronic record, means a person who, on behalf of another person, sends, receives or stores that electronic record or provides other services with respect to that electronic record.

Question: description: Lack of transparent technical standards
Source Legislation:
Bureau of Standards Act No.14 of 2016;

Telecommunications, Radiocommunications and Broadcasting Type Approval and Conformity to Technical Standards Order No.191 of 2018
Impact:
There are no complaints about lack of foreign participation in standard-setting bodies for telecom products or of non-transparent standards. Vanuatu Standard is based on international best practises and harmonised with relevant international or regional standards (Section 16.2). A draft standard shall be published as a notice in a local newspaper and by other means to notify the public (Section 16.5). A person within 60 days may submit a written objection (Section 16.6).

In particular, the Order No.191 states that the radiocommunications device manufactured domestically or imported into the country must conform to the applicable technical standards (Section 3).
Timeframe for Indicator:

Question: description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
Source Legislation: Telecommunications, Radiocommunications and Broadcasting Type Approval and Conformity to Technical Standards Order No.191 of 2018
Impact:
SDoC is not implemented in Vanuatu. However, Vanuatu recognizes the  3rd party-certification (Section 15 of the 2018 Order). The list of the recognized certification bodies (CABs) can be found in Schedule 2, including Australia, China, European Union, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, the Republic of Korea, the United States, Hong Kong; China, and Taiwan Province of China.

Local importers need to obtain type approval import permits from the Telecommunications, Radiocommunications & Broadcasting Regulator for the approval of importation, use and for sale of any ICT equipment each time a consignment of relevant equipment is imported to Vanuatu.

Question: description: Product screening and testing requirements
Source Legislation: Telecommunications, Radiocommunications and Broadcasting Type Approval and Conformity to Technical Standards Order No.191 of 2018
Impact:
Vanuatu does not require local laboratory testing or screening. 

If the record does not provides sufficient evidence, the regulator may require the suppliers in writing to submit a test report from a conformity assessment body recognized by one of the recognized certification bodies stating that the device conforms with each applicable standards; or a written statement from a conformity assessment body (CAB) recognized by one of the recognized certification bodies certifying that the device conforms with one or more requirements in an applicable standard (Section 15(1). A supplier must submit the request within 30 days (Section 15(2)).

Question: description: Low De Minimis

Impact: Vanuatu has no de minimis threshold, which means that there is no minimum value below which a good is exempted from duties and taxes collected by customs.

Question: description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
Source Legislation:
E-Business Act [Cap 264] of 2000;

Companies Act 2012
Impact: Counterparty or cyber suite proprietor is not required: (I) to be licensed under any Act or other law of Vanuatu to carry on business in or within Vanuatu; or (ii) to obtain any other permission or authority under any Act or other law of Vanuatu to carry on business in or within Vanuatu, by reason only of the creation, entry into, effecting, purchase, sale or issue of an electronic business contract or cyber suite contract (Section 5 of the E-Business Act). Note that a company is defined as international company [Cap 222 ] that do not require local presence (Section 1).

Question: description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
Impact:
Vanuatu does not have a general consumer protection law. The consumer protection can be found under sectoral laws, including the Telecommunications and Radiocommunications Regulation Act 2009, the Utilities Regulatory Authority Act 2007; the Food (Control) Act 1993; and the Weights Act. 

Specifically, the Telecommunication and Radiocommunications Regulation provides online consumer protection in the telecom market (Part 8 Consumer relations and protection). For example, a service provider must establish procedures to deal with disputes and complaints from end-users (Section 41). Moreover, the order subsequently issued in 2015 prescribes online consumer protection in detail, such as the authorized uses and disclosure of consumer information, and online advertising.
Timeframe for Indicator:
Since November 2009, last amended in 2018;

Since October 2015
